content: For individuals living with HIV, a comprehensive approach to sexual and reproductive health should include appropriate STI screening and treatment services. Regular screening and treatment for STIs are essential for people living with HIV. Men who have sex with men and transgender individuals presenting with symptomatic STIs should receive syndromic management and treatment in accordance with WHO guidelines. Where feasible, etiological diagnosis should also be pursued. To prevent future STIs, promoting safer sexual practices, including consistent condom use, is critical. Specific recommendations exist for managing each syndrome. Anorectal symptoms and infections are common among individuals engaging in anal intercourse, including men who have sex with men, sex workers, transgender individuals, and women who have had receptive anal intercourse with partners with STIs. Asymptomatic anorectal infections are also not uncommon, though precise data are limited. These infections may present with symptoms such as anorectal pain, itching, discharge, bleeding, rectal fullness, tenesmus, constipation, or mucus-streaked stools. For pregnant women with syphilis and cases of congenital syphilis, updated treatment guidelines were published in 2016. Integrating STI services into HIV care settings is a key strategy to improve access to testing, treatment, and prevention services for people living with HIV. Addressing stigma and discrimination is essential to encourage health-seeking behavior and improve public health efforts to control HIV and STI epidemics. Research is needed to better understand how to promote sexual health effectively, especially given advancements in HIV treatment, diagnostic capabilities, and digital education tools. Vaccination is an important component of HIV care. People living with HIV should be assessed for vaccine eligibility at all stages of care. Vaccines are generally more effective and safer for individuals on antiretroviral therapy (ART) with stable immune function (CD4 count >200 cells/mm³). However, those with severe immunosuppression may face higher risks from live attenuated vaccines. Inactivated vaccines, while safe, may require additional doses or revaccination after immune reconstitution. For COVID-19, WHO-recommended vaccines are considered safe for people living with HIV, with no reported interactions between these vaccines and antiretroviral drugs. Vaccination should continue alongside ART to maintain health. Specific vaccine recommendations for people living with HIV include: BCG vaccine: Safe for children on ART with stable immune function. Neonates of unknown HIV status should be vaccinated unless clinical evidence suggests HIV infection. Hepatitis B vaccine: Higher dosages may elicit stronger immune responses in people living with HIV. Tetanus-containing vaccines: Suitable for immunocompromised individuals, though immune responses may be lower. Measles vaccine: Recommended for asymptomatic individuals and those with mild symptomatic HIV infection. In high-incidence areas, an initial dose may be given as early as six months of age. HPV vaccine: Should be introduced as part of cervical cancer prevention strategies, targeting girls aged 9–14 years before sexual activity begins. Cholera vaccine: Oral cholera vaccines are safe and beneficial for people living with HIV, including pregnant and lactating women. Dengue vaccine: Not recommended for individuals with symptomatic HIV or impaired immune function. Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine: Infants living with HIV may benefit from a booster dose in their second year of life. Rubella vaccine: Contraindicated for individuals with severe immunodeficiency, including symptomatic HIV infection. Typhoid vaccine: Safe for immunologically stable individuals living with HIV, though immune responses depend on CD4 count. HIV infection increases the prevalence and severity of skin and oral conditions, particularly as CD4 counts decline below 200 cells/mm³. Up to 90% of individuals with HIV in resource-limited settings experience these conditions, which can exacerbate stigma and discrimination. Common conditions include Kaposi’s sarcoma, seborrheic dermatitis, herpes zoster, and oral candidiasis. ART is the primary treatment for many of these conditions. Nutritional care is critical for people living with HIV, as the infection can lead to weight loss, wasting, and malnutrition due to increased energy demands, reduced appetite, and nutrient losses. Nutritional assessment and support should be integrated into HIV care, with food supplements provided in food-insecure contexts. For children, optimal feeding practices, including exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months, followed by complementary feeding, are essential. Breastfeeding remains a cornerstone of child survival and maternal health. WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding for six months, followed by continued breastfeeding with complementary foods for up to two years or beyond. ART reduces the risk of postnatal HIV transmission, even in mixed feeding contexts. Breastfeeding should only cease when a nutritionally adequate and safe diet without breast milk can be provided. Data collection on breastfeeding duration, ART adherence, and retention in care is essential to improve service delivery.
